## Purpose

This report examines how average BMI differs across income groups among adults aged 20–80 in the prepared NHANES Health Equity classroom dataset. I used a summary table and visualization to look at these differences and better understand the patterns in the data. Since the analysis is descriptive and does not account for NHANES survey weights, the findings are intended to show patterns within this dataset rather than represent the US population. 
This is a practice report using the prepared NHANES classroom dataset rather than my group's project data.

## Question

How does mean BMI vary by income group among adults age 20-80 in the prepared NHANES Health Equity classroom dataset?

## Data Source

The report uses the cached CSV snapshot at `examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv`. The source data are derived from CDC/NCHS NHANES public-use files [@cdc-nhanes].

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)  # AI-EDIT(2026-06-23): tidyverse-default — consolidated core library() calls into library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

candidate_paths <- c(
  "examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
  "../../examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
  "../../../examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv"
)

data_path <- candidate_paths[file.exists(candidate_paths)][1]
if (is.na(data_path)) {
  stop("Could not find examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv")
}

nhanes <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Methods

I used the prepared NHANES Health Equity classroom dataset and restricted the analysis to adults aged 20–80. I first checked for missing values in BMI, income group, and age. For the comparison, I excluded records with missing BMI or income group values and calculated the number of participants, mean BMI, and standard deviation for each income group.

The summary table and figure were generated using R. Since the analysis is unweighted and descriptive, the findings cannot be used to represent the US population or establish a causal relationship between income and BMI.

```{r}
analysis_df <- nhanes |>
  filter(Age >= 20, Age <= 80)

missingness <- analysis_df |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    missing_bmi = sum(is.na(BMI)),
    missing_income = sum(is.na(IncomeGroup)),
    missing_age = sum(is.na(Age))
  )

kable(missingness, caption = "Missingness check for key report variables.")
```

## Results

```{r}
income_summary <- analysis_df |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup)) |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI),
    sd_bmi = sd(BMI),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `BMI, mean (SD)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean_bmi, sd_bmi)
  ) |>
  select(IncomeGroup, n, `BMI, mean (SD)`)

kable(income_summary, caption = "Descriptive BMI summary by income group.")
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Mean BMI by income group among adults age 20-80 in the prepared NHANES Health Equity classroom dataset. Values are unweighted and descriptive."
plot_df <- analysis_df |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup)) |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMI),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = IncomeGroup, y = mean_bmi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean BMI by income group",
    subtitle = "Adults age 20-80; unweighted descriptive summary",
    x = "Income group",
    y = "Mean BMI"
  ) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The results show some differences in average BMI across the three income groups. The low-income group had the highest mean BMI at 29.4, followed closely by the middle-income group at 29.3. The high-income group had a slightly lower mean BMI of 28.6.

Although the differences between the groups were relatively small, the pattern suggests that BMI may vary with income in this dataset. However, the results alone cannot explain why these differences exist or whether income itself contributes to them. Other factors that were not examined in this analysis may also play a role.

## Limitations

Although the table and figure show differences in average BMI between income groups, there are some limitations to consider. This analysis uses a prepared classroom dataset and does not account for NHANES survey weights, so the findings cannot be used to represent the US population. Participants with missing BMI or income group values were also excluded, which may affect the patterns observed.

The analysis also does not account for other factors that may be related to BMI, such as age differences, access to healthcare, or living conditions. Overall, the results can help identify patterns within the dataset, but they cannot explain what is causing those differences.

## Plain-Language Summary

The low-income group had a slightly higher average BMI (29.4) compared to the high-income group (28.6). The difference was relatively small, but it raises questions about how income and other social factors might relate to health.

I think it's important to recognize that these findings only show a pattern within the classroom dataset. The results don't tell us why these differences exist or whether income itself plays a role. They do provide a starting point for understanding how health outcomes may differ across income groups.
